original.reason: It does not justify that an arbitrary chain has an upper bound: condition (ii) concerns countable divisibility sequences, not chains as stated. More importantly, after showing minimal elements are associate, it never proves that every element of I is divisible by the selected minimal element, so I=(a) does not follow.

judgment.reason: The essential ideal argument is correct once a maximal class exists, but the claimed Zorn hypothesis is not rigorously established. An arbitrary chain cannot simply be represented by a divisibility sequence; a separate argument is needed that a chain without a maximal element yields a countable strictly increasing subchain contradicting (ii).

The use of Zorn's lemma has a material gap: condition (ii) applies only to sequences, whereas the proof asserts without justification that every possibly uncountable chain can be arranged as such a sequence.

The proof correctly derives I=(a) from a maximal class, but does not rigorously prove that every chain has an upper bound. The unsupported reduction of an arbitrary chain to a divisibility sequence is insufficient.

It contains the same unproved Zorn prerequisite: an arbitrary chain need not itself be a sequence, and condition (ii) alone is not directly the asserted chain upper-bound statement without an additional construction.
